analysis.one_liner: Raises oil companies' liability for spill damages and strengthens compensation and safety rules after the Gulf oil disaster.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any of the six committees it was sent to and died with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in response to the Deepwater Horizon explosion, this bill would have roughly quadrupled the liability cap for offshore oil spills (from $75 million to $300 million), required the government to pay spill victims any damages the responsible company could not cover, and backfilled the fund with a new levy on the oil industry. It also would have raised the per-barrel tax that finances oil spill cleanup, given offshore rig workers and victims' families stronger rights to sue, required vetted and redundant oil spill response plans, and let regulators suspend drilling permits after repeated safety violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing and tourism businesses, and families of workers killed offshore would gain stronger and faster compensation after a spill, including new rights to sue for non-economic losses and punitive damages in cases of gross negligence. Offshore rig workers would gain the right to sue their employer for injuries, and taxpayers would be partly shielded because a new industry levy would cover damages that exceed the company's liability cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf Coast residents and spill victims

how_it_helps.text: Raises the liability cap for offshore facility spills from $75 million to $300 million and requires the government to pay victims any damages above what the responsible party must cover, first from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund and then from a levy on the oil industry [S2] [S3].

Extends Jones Act injury rights to workers on offshore drilling facilities and lets surviving spouses, parents, children, siblings, and dependent relatives sue the employer or anyone whose act or omission caused the injury or death [S2] [S3].

Amends the Death on the High Seas Act so families can recover nonpecuniary damages (loss of care, comfort, and companionship), compensation for the decedent's pain and suffering, and punitive damages in cases of gross negligence or willful misconduct [S3].

Raises the per-barrel tax that finances the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund from 8 to 30 cents (and 9 to 40 cents for some crude), makes the tax permanent, and raises the fund's per-incident spending caps from $1 billion to $10 billion for cleanup [S3].

Requires oil spill response plans to include backup actions if the primary plan fails and to be vetted by impartial experts, bars new outer Continental Shelf drilling permits without an approved response plan, and allows suspension of drilling operations after five or more safety violations in a year [S2] [S3].

Directs the oil industry to establish a $1 billion research fund for spill recovery and cleanup technology, and directs the government to make PTSD counseling available to victims of major oil spills, including people who suffered severe economic losses [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies would bear the costs: a fourfold-higher liability cap, a new industry levy to cover damages beyond the caps, a much higher per-barrel excise tax, a $1 billion research fund, and stricter response-plan and permitting requirements. Some of the excise tax would likely be passed through to consumers at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps a liability cap in place and has the government pay victims for damages above it, then tries to recover from an industry levy, which could leave taxpayers exposed if the levy proves difficult to collect [S2] [S3].

Raising the spill tax to 30-40 cents a barrel and quadrupling liability exposure would raise operating costs for domestic offshore drilling, costs that could be passed to consumers or push drilling toward laxer foreign jurisdictions, an objection the oil industry made against similar post-spill proposals.

The bill restricts recovery by noncitizen and nonresident alien workers injured during international voyages of foreign vessels, narrowing rights for a group of maritime workers even as it expands rights for others [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Gulf Coast communities and spill victims, the benefits are substantial: faster guaranteed compensation, broader family recovery, and real safety checks on deepwater drilling. The main costs fall on oil companies, and some would flow to consumers through higher fuel prices; the government-backstop structure also carries some taxpayer risk if the industry levy falls short. On balance the bill tilts clearly toward protecting people over protecting drillers, though it was introduced late in the session with no cosponsors and no committee movement, so it never faced the scrutiny that might have refined its weakest provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2010, referred to six committees and three subcommittees, none of which ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011 without a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on July 1, 2010, about ten weeks after the Deepwater Horizon explosion, and it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Ways and Means, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Science and Technology committees [S1] [S5].

Within days it was sent to three subcommittees — Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, Water Resources and Environment, and Energy and Mineral Resources — but the record shows no hearings, no markups, and no floor action after that referral [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors [S4], and it died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies are better off: the offshore liability cap stayed at $75 million, the spill-financing excise tax stayed near 8-9 cents a barrel, and no new safety or claims requirements took effect. Spill victims and coastal communities remain under the pre-2010 rules.

for.name: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House committees of referral (Transportation and Infrastructure, Ways and Means, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Science and Technology)
against.role: Committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the referral and subcommittee assignments; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed post-Deepwater Horizon proposals to lift or multiply the offshore liability cap and raise spill-related taxes and permitting requirements.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split cannot be measured; the bill's sole sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have quadrupled their offshore liability cap, imposed a new industry levy and a much higher per-barrel spill tax, and subjected them to stricter response-plan and permitting rules. Their interest in blocking it ran against the interest of coastal residents and spill victims in fuller compensation and tighter safety oversight.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast fishing, shrimping, and tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses bore the economic losses from the Deepwater Horizon spill, and the bill would have required claims to be processed with fishermen treated as a separate category and created an independent claims system and PTSD counseling for economic victims. Their fortunes rise and fall with the wellbeing of Gulf communities.

industries.industry: Maritime and offshore drilling contractors and vessel operators
industries.note: Extending the Jones Act to offshore facility workers and expanding Death on the High Seas Act damages would have widened their exposure to injury and death lawsuits from crew and rig workers.
